results.title: NCAR HPC Documentation - Determining computational resource needs
results.content: Documenting your code’s performance and scalability to demonstrate that your stated resource needs are reasonable is an important aspect of preparing an allocation request. While performing benchmark runs on Derecho is strongly recommended, if you have core-hour costs from Cheyenne benchmark runs, you can estimate Derecho CPU performance by multiplying by **0.77**. We encourage researchers to estimate GPU-hour needs by making test/benchmark runs on Derecho or Casper GPUs, but we will accept estimates based on runs on comparable non-NSF NCAR, GPU-based systems. If you are using codes or models that do not have well-known performance information, you will need to document the performance and scalability of your codes to complete your resource request. Presumably you’ve run your code on a multi-core or GPU system and have at least a general idea of what resources you will need in order to run at the same scale or larger on the Derecho or Casper systems. Document your code’s performance with test runs on the Derecho system if possible, or on a reasonably similar platform and software stack. You will want to illustrate in a graph that your code performs well at increasingly higher scale, showing **at least four points** indicating the results of your runs (as in Figure 1). If your application’s performance is not already well documented, you may need to establish a baseline by running it on a single node before scaling. For example, say you’ve run your parallel code on a similar system using 4,000 cores, or you’ve had an opportunity to do some similar-size test runs on Derecho. To convert that into total core-hours needed for one type of simulation, multiply core-hours per simulation (the time needed to complete one simulation times the number of cores used) by the number of times you are proposing to run that type of simulation. As you do your test runs, keep in mind that strong scaling – the degree to which performance improves as more processors are applied to a **fixed problem size** – is more useful for these purposes than weak scaling, which reflects the ability to solve larger problem sizes with more processors. If you identify such a point in your test runs, it would make little sense to base your allocation request on higher numbers of cores.

results.title: [2501.08737] Resource-Constrained Federated Continual Learning: What Does Matter?
results.content: Submitted on 15 Jan 2025 ([v1), last revised 14 Oct 2025 (this version, v2)]. # Title:Resource-Constrained Federated Continual Learning: What Does Matter? Authors:Yichen Li, Yuying Wang, Jiahua Dong, Haozhao Wang, Yining Qi, Rui Zhang, Ruixuan Li. View a PDF of the paper titled Resource-Constrained Federated Continual Learning: What Does Matter?, by Yichen Li and 6 other authors. > Abstract:Federated Continual Learning (FCL) aims to enable sequentially privacy-preserving model training on streams of incoming data that vary in edge devices by preserving previous knowledge while adapting to new data. Current FCL literature focuses on restricted data privacy and access to previously seen data while imposing no constraints on the training overhead. This is unreasonable for FCL applications in real-world scenarios, where edge devices are primarily constrained by resources such as storage, computational budget, and label rate. We revisit this problem with a large-scale benchmark and analyze the performance of state-of-the-art FCL approaches under different resource-constrained settings. Various typical FCL techniques and six datasets in two incremental learning scenarios (Class-IL and Domain-IL) are involved in our experiments. Through extensive experiments amounting to a total of over 1,000+ GPU hours, we find that, under limited resource-constrained settings, existing FCL approaches, with no exception, fail to achieve the expected performance. This suggests that most existing FCL methods are particularly too resource-dependent for real-world deployment. Moreover, we study the performance of typical FCL techniques with resource constraints and shed light on future research directions in FCL. **** Wed, 15 Jan 2025 11:33:52 UTC (1,048 KB). **[v2]** Tue, 14 Oct 2025 12:56:02 UTC (196 KB). ## Access Paper:. results.title: Vendors for a server used in computational biology | Ars OpenForum
results.content: I'm in need of a new server for a lab, where we process and analyze genetic data (RNA-seq, whole-genome assembly, etc.) Since we process a lot of samples, and the computational pipelines need fairly beefy hardware, it makes more sense to have a server in-house as opposed to using cloud services. However, the quote they recently gave me for an AMD Epyc 9334 based system (32 Cores, 64GB RAM) was painfully high, mostly due to the large SSD RAID (due to tariffs, ultimately.) A similar, slightly better system (with 755GB RAM!) cost ~18.5k about 1.5 years ago, but now they charge 29k. * 300\*80 / 60 = 400 hours < 17 days to run on the newer machine (AMD EPYC 9334, 1 Processor, 32 Cores, 3.91 GHz, much better data I/O performance due to SSD RAID). Consumer machines packed with memory are very cost effective with 64GB modules, I say as someone who recently priced out options for high memory systems (in my case, a novel AI model type I am currently developing, which is high memory use and cannot easily run on a GPU.). If you want to do GPU for AI, HBAs for storage (even if they are sata/sas drives) and 100gb network cards, you run out of lanes really quick in the consumer lines. Cloud storage is stupidly expensive at these scales, assuming it's anything like the kind of sequencing projects I've worked on - TBs per project, totals in the PB range, and data kept for years. Cloud compute is all about peaky use - if you need a steady level of compute 24x7, buy servers - payback is in the 3-6 month range. 1x 4TB SSD "Input Data" drive. Your protection is the multiple storage locations and if the "Input Data" drive fails, you can restore from the Synology copy onto the replacement SSD or repurpose the Offload drive temporarily. On the compute side, typically we use supermicro, asus or gigabyte, depending on exact needs and relative pricing - we go quad node in 2U for CPU compute nodes up to 1TB RAM, but 2U or bigger for GPU based or big memory nodes.

results.title: Taming the Chaos of Computational Experiments | SIAM
results.content: Today’s computational experiments form the basis of scientific simulations and data analysis methods that will fuel future scientific advancements, engineering-based designs and evaluations, government policy decisions, and much more. As part of this discussion, I hope that we also consider the importance of involving *all* authors in computational experiments. While each author need not necessarily write their own code and run it independently, everyone should *understand* the experiments — the inputs, codes, individual outputs, and summary results. In this article, I will share seven pragmatic practices for improving the replicability, validation, reproducibility, and usability of computational experiments. A common pitfall in computational experiments is the *direct* generation of figures from experimental runs. In addition to saving data files for the production of figures, I advocate for saving detailed, human-digestible logs of your experiments by tooling your scripts and codes to print regular status messages. I address logs in more detail in the next point, but here I want to stress that you and your coauthors should be able to read through these records to better understand your computational experiment. Besides being digestible by humans, your logs should include the necessary details to reproduce individual experiments. * Git hashes for code and data (and diff logs if you don’t commit before every run). Scripts allow you to rerun experiments after code changes, perform parameter sweeps, incorporate feedback from collaborators and/or referees, and apply the same methods to new datasets or scenarios. A well-organized set of scripts can preprocess raw input data, recreate individual runs, regenerate all runs, collate results, and generate figures. * **Outputs:** Various outputs of the computational experiments, such as (i) *logs:* numerous human-readable summaries from individual experiments; (ii) *raw data:* machine-readable data files from individual experiments; and (iii) *summaries:* aggregated results used in figures and tables. #### Share Your Code, Data, and Experimental Logs. I would also argue for the importance of sharing the input data and output logs of computational experiments. Sharing codes, data, and experimental logs is beneficial for science and fosters transparency, collaboration, and scientific progress.
